This is an instructional notebook. It is notebook 4, the last notebook of part 1 (regression on hourly bike rentals) of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL".

Content: an 80 percent prediction interval (PI) should catch 80 percent of unseen hours; coverage measures the fraction it catches. HGBT gives a PI by fitting one model per quantile under the pinball loss (quantiles 0.1 and 0.9), wrapped in a small estimator whose `predict` returns both bounds. TabICL needs no loss and no second fit: it holds a distribution of plausible values per row, and `predict(X, output_type="quantiles", alphas=[0.1, 0.9])` reads the bounds from it, with `n_estimators=1`. The data stops at the end of its longest gap-free stretch (see datasets_bike_sharing), so test windows span consecutive hours.

Results of the reference run: on the last fold, HGBT's PI misses most commute peaks while TabICL's stretches to meet them and stays tighter elsewhere. Over the 10 folds, scored with `make_scorer` for coverage, mean width and the average pinball loss of both bounds, TabICL lands within a point of 80 percent coverage, HGBT catches around 60 percent, and TabICL's PI is also narrower on average, so HGBT is wider and less trustworthy at once. Coverage and width must be read together, since any PI can raise coverage by growing; the pinball loss scores both and ranks the models the same way. With `max_train_size=2400` (two folds, same 400 test hours as the last two folds), HGBT's coverage rises by more than ten points, partly by widening, but stays short of TabICL on 800 rows; TabICL barely moves.

Why TabICL's PI is better calibrated: both models are trained with the pinball loss, but on different rows. HGBT minimizes it on its 800 training rows, which its trees already fit, so its bounds are sized for training errors and too narrow on test hours. TabICL minimized it during pretraining on rows held out of each synthetic table's context, so its PIs account for noise and for uncertainty about the relationship, which is the situation of our test hours. HGBT could be tuned on validation folds, but they would come from the same 800 rows. Also, HGBT's two bounds are separate models and can cross (on a few quiet night hours), while TabICL's 999 quantiles come from one distribution and cannot cross. TabICL's PI can be narrower and calibrated because its forecasts are closer to the truth.

Place in the course: last notebook of part 1. The same argument about held-out rows returns in TabICL_calibration for classifier probabilities; questions on classifier calibration get a short answer and a pointer there. Related scikit-learn course material: regression metrics and time series cross-validation (Evaluating Model Performance), gradient boosting (Ensemble Models).
